title: 残業なし、交互に育休　「無理しない」スウェーデンの子育て事情

translated_text: In Sweden, one of the world's most gender-equal countries, the amount of time men spend on housework and childcare is more than three times that of Japan. From the life of Yoshihiro Sato (47), a resident of Sweden who has also written books about child-rearing, we explore the differences in work styles and systems that support work-life balance. They live in a multi-family housing complex built in 2017, facing a large park, with daycare and elementary school within a 5-minute walk. They live with his wife Yoko (44), their 8-year-old eldest son, and 1-year-old second son. When we visited in December last year, Yoko was on parental leave. Yoshihiro works as a data scientist at a bank. In the morning, he drops his eldest son off at elementary school and arrives at work around 8:30 AM. He picks up his son around 4 PM and returns home to work for about an hour. He works from home three days a week. No overtime, free vocational training, complete public childcare, gender equality, and flat interpersonal relationships - these are vastly different from Japan. What stands out is that it's not just about the systems, but fundamentally different perspectives on what it means to be human, to live, and what government should be. Sweden also had a different situation in the past. Regarding so-called 'job-based' versus 'membership-based' employment, we explain these to students every year, focusing on whether there are personnel transfers, and have them discuss and write about which is better. title_en: No Overtime, Alternating Parental Leave: The 'No-Rushing' Child-Rearing Way in Sweden
